title: Gradient descent, how neural networks learn | Deep Learning Chapter 2
beats: Recap network structure; two goals: gradient descent, then what hidden layers look for
Digits on 28x28 grid, 784 inputs, 13,000 weights and biases, brightest output wins
Goal: show labeled training data, adjust weights, test on unseen data; MNIST
Learning is just a calculus exercise: minimize a function; start random
Scold the random output ('bad computer'); cost is sum of squared differences
Cost function takes 13,000 inputs, one output; too much to imagine
Zoom to one-input function: step by slope sign, ball rolling downhill
Many valleys; local minimum not guaranteed best; step proportional to slope avoids overshoot
Two inputs: surface over xy-plane; downhill direction is negative gradient
You only need that such a vector exists; fine if multivariable calculus is shaky
Same idea in 13,000 dimensions; backprop deferred to next video
Name: gradient descent; smooth cost is why activations are continuous
Second reading of gradient: components as relative importance (3 times bang for buck)
Three layered functions: network, cost, gradient of cost
96% accuracy, 98% with tweaks; but hidden neurons look random, not edges
Random noise input gets confident answer; network cannot draw digits
Why introduce edges motivation: starting point, old technology
Pause and think how to make it detect edges; Nielsen book, Olah
Interview clip: random-label memorization vs structured data learns faster, minima of equal quality

theory: The video drops dimensions to recover intuition: solve the 1-input case, then 2-input, then assert the same recipe works in 13,000, and explicitly reduces the required math to 'a downhill vector exists'. It then shows the honest negative result (random-looking weights, confident noise) to prevent an overclaimed mental model.
